doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Union presidents and the abolition of the Oakland office
summary: After Pop Kennedy, weaker presidents close the Oakland office, membership falls, and he becomes assistant in San Francisco.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: So Pop Kennedy passed away in 1967 then we had another president, kind of a weak president. Kennedy was a strong labor man. He knew all the delegates from our various labor councils and he was on the Executive Board of the American Federation of Musicians. He was a strong labor man. Then when he passed Al Arnold ascended. Al wasn’t very assertive. And so then in 1972 we had another president Jerry Spain. He ascended to the presidency. He had gone to law school and he became president. Well he didn’t like Oakland. Never did like Oakland. So he talked the Board of Directors into abolishing the Oakland office. They did it by Board resolution and then that same year, © Fillius Jazz Archive -30-

election, they put it on the ballot to officially abolish the office, and put it up to a vote. And of course they voted, the membership voted to abolish the office. And that was very crucial and very damaging. Because we had about a third of our membership lived in the East Bay. And many of them held dual memberships. Local 424 was the Richmond Local, 510 was the San Leandro Local. And many of the fellas held dual membership. So they considered that Oakland office their office. They’d come in to pay their dues or just come in to gab. And when we had the elections — we had machine elections at that time — elections by machine. Now we have mail ballot. Anyhow during election time oh they’d set up in this particular building, they had a large room, almost like a ballroom, and they’d set up the voting booths and the fellas would come and it would be like a party. Because they’d be handshaking, just like a funeral the way the people gather, only it was very cheerful and convivial and all of that. And so they felt, man, you’re taking away our office. So unfortunately many of them resigned. That was the beginning of the exodus out. And so now we’re down to around about, tops, 3000 members. From 6,500 in 1965. So anyhow the office, they closed the office so then I ended up in San Francisco as an assistant to the Secretary/Treasurer. So I was over there from ’72 until ’94 I guess, and then another new administration came in and then they reduced the office staff. And so I ran for the Board of Directors. First time out I was elected. So this is my third two year term.
